paper.title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

A.label: Without review
A.note: reconcile only

B.label: With external review

rows.claim: Being the decision-maker (Social + Solo vs Partner condition) reduces participant happiness independently of outcome (Study 1: t(3600)=−3.92, p<0.0001, β=−0.14, 95%CI=[−0.20, −0.07]; Study 2: t(2870)=−6.07, p<0.0001, β=−0.24, 95%CI=[−0.31, −0.16]), consistent with a psychological cost of assuming responsibility for others.

A.claim: Happiness was lower when the participant rather than the partner made the choice, independent of the outcome (Study 1: t(3600) = –3.92, p < 0.0001, β = –0.14; Study 2: t(2870) = –6.07, p < 0.0001, β = –0.24).
A.note: same agency main effect, identical stats

B.claim: Happiness was lower when the participant rather than the partner made the choice, independent of the outcome (Study 1: t(3600) = –3.92, p < 0.0001, β = –0.14; Study 2: t(2870) = –6.07, p < 0.0001, β = –0.24).
B.note: same agency main effect, identical stats

rows.claim: The happiness cost observed in the Social condition is general agency aversion — the unpleasantness of being the decision-maker as such — and is not contingent on responsibility for a negative outcome befalling the partner.

The happiness decrease following negative partner outcomes under participant choice is driven by the participant's own lottery outcome rather than by the partner's, and so reflects self-directed disappointment rather than interpersonal guilt.
The imaging pipeline and condition contrasts do not recover established effects, so differences reported between Social and Partner conditions cannot be attributed to the experimental manipulation.

The model-based fMRI approach does not recover known neural signals, so parametric modulators derived from the computational model — including the partner reward prediction error regressors — cannot be trusted.
Participants did not engage with the lottery task in a value-sensitive way — choices were inattentive or random — so the behavioural measures carry no information about preference or affect.

The happiness and choice differences between Social and Partner conditions reflect a social-context-driven shift in risk attitude — participants become more or less risk averse when choosing on another person's behalf — rather than responsibility-contingent interpersonal guilt.

B.claim: Making choices that affect a partner as well as oneself changes the risk preferences people reveal, relative to choosing for themselves alone.
B.note: social context changes revealed risk preferences

rows.claim: The guilt effect (happiness decrease after low partner outcomes under participant vs partner choice) is present regardless of whether the participant received the high or low lottery outcome: high own outcome: Study 1 t(39)=−3.58, p<0.001, d=0.56, BF10=32; Study 2 t(43)=−2.68, p=0.01, d=0.40, BF10=3.8; low own outcome: Study 1 t(39)=−3.39, p=0.002, d=0.54, BF10=19; Study 2 t(43)=−3.58, p<0.001, d=0.54, BF10=33.5.

A.claim: The guilt effect occurred whether the participant received the high lottery outcome themselves (Study 1: t(39) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.56, BF10 = 32; Study 2: t(43) = –2.68, p = 0.01, d = 0.4, BF10 = 3.8) or the low lottery outcome (Study 1: t(39) = –3.39, p = 0.002, d = 0.54, BF10 = 19; Study 2: t(43) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.54, BF10 = 33.5).
A.note: guilt effect regardless of own outcome

B.claim: The guilt effect occurred whether the participant received the high lottery outcome themselves (Study 1: t(39) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.56, BF10 = 32; Study 2: t(43) = –2.68, p = 0.01, d = 0.4, BF10 = 3.8) or the low lottery outcome (Study 1: t(39) = –3.39, p = 0.002, d = 0.54, BF10 = 19; Study 2: t(43) = –3.58, p < 0.001, d = 0.54, BF10 = 33.5).
B.note: guilt effect regardless of own outcome

rows.claim: Happiness ratings decrease more after negative partner outcomes when the participant made the choice (Social condition) than when the partner made the choice (Partner condition), operationalizing interpersonal guilt as responsibility-contingent unhappiness about partner harm.

A.claim: Participants felt worse following low lottery outcomes for the partner when those outcomes were consequences of their own choice rather than the partner's, which the authors interpret as interpersonal guilt.
A.note: responsibility-contingent unhappiness after partner loss

B.claim: Participants felt worse following low lottery outcomes for the partner when those outcomes were consequences of their own choice rather than the partner's, which the authors interpret as interpersonal guilt.
B.note: responsibility-contingent unhappiness after partner loss

rows.claim: Individual dot-product values between participants' guilt-related BOLD responses and the Yu & Koban neural guilt signature do not correlate with individual behavioral guilt effect scores (Spearman's Rho=−0.058, p=0.725), indicating the neural signature does not track individual differences in guilt sensitivity as measured behaviorally.

A.claim: Inter-individual differences in guilt-signature dot product values did not correlate with the behavioural guilt responses (Spearman's Rho = –0.058, p = 0.725).
A.note: same null correlation, Rho=-0.058

B.claim: Inter-individual differences in guilt-signature dot product values did not correlate with the behavioural guilt responses (Spearman's Rho = –0.058, p = 0.725).
B.note: same null correlation, Rho=-0.058

rows.claim: Participant momentary happiness correlates with both participant reward (Study 1: F(1,3598)=691.5, R²=0.16; Study 2: F(1,2630)=650.8, R²=0.20) and partner reward (Study 1: F(1,2426)=128.6, R²=0.05; Study 2: F(1,1735)=111.8, R²=0.06), confirming that participants were emotionally responsive to partner outcomes throughout the task.

A.claim: In Study 1, participants' momentary happiness varied with the rewards received by their partner (F(1,2426) = 128.6, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.05).
A.note: happiness tracks partner reward, same F

B.claim: In Study 1, participants' momentary happiness varied with the rewards received by their partner (F(1,2426) = 128.6, p < 0.001, R2 = 0.05).
B.note: happiness tracks partner reward, same F

rows.claim: Anterior insula is the neural substrate of interpersonal guilt: when a participant bears responsibility for a choice that yields a negative outcome for another person, anterior insula activity tracks the resulting responsibility-contingent affect. The region is recruited specifically by the conjunction of self-agency over the choice and harm to the partner, distinguishing guilt from generic empathy for partner loss (which would be present in the Partner condition too) and from regret about one's own loss (which would be present in Solo trials too).

Momentary happiness in social decision contexts is governed by a computational rule in which partner reward prediction errors that arise from the participant's own choices (social_pRPEs) carry an independent, non-zero weight, distinct from the weight on partner RPEs that arise without participant agency. Responsibility modulates how partner outcomes enter the happiness computation: participants internalize partner losses as affective costs specifically when those losses can be attributed to their own decision.

A.claim: Responsibility for a reward — whether it followed a choice made by the participant or by the partner — influences variations in the participant's momentary happiness.
A.note: responsibility for reward modulates happiness

B.claim: Responsibility for a reward — whether it followed a choice made by the participant or by the partner — influences variations in the participant's momentary happiness.
B.note: responsibility for reward modulates happiness

rows.claim: Superior temporal sulcus (STS) — a core mentalizing-network region — represents the partner's affective experience specifically when the participant is responsible for the partner's outcome. The mentalizing computation is conditioned on agency: STS does not track partner reward prediction errors uniformly, but rather engages selectively when the participant's own choice produced the partner's outcome, consistent with self-attributed responsibility recruiting other-modeling.

A.claim: This region of the left superior temporal sulcus tracks a partner's unexpected outcomes less when they do not follow from the participant's decisions.
A.note: STS tracking conditional on participant agency

B.claim: This region of the left superior temporal sulcus tracks a partner's unexpected outcomes less when they do not follow from the participant's decisions.
B.note: STS tracking conditional on participant agency

rows.claim: The anterior insula guilt effect is consistent with a previously published neural guilt signature map (Yu & Koban), providing convergent validity for the insula as a guilt-tracking region.

A.claim: Dot products between individual neural responses to low partner outcomes and the published multivariate guilt-related brain signature were overall positive (mean = 5.22; median = 6.97; sign test p = 0.017; Cliff's Delta = 0.4).
A.note: positive alignment with published guilt signature

B.claim: Dot products between individual neural responses to low partner outcomes and the published multivariate guilt-related brain signature were overall positive (mean = 5.22; median = 6.97; sign test p = 0.017; Cliff's Delta = 0.4).
B.note: positive alignment with published guilt signature

rows.claim: Functional connectivity (gPPI) between anterior insula and inferior frontal gyrus varies by experimental condition, with increased coupling in the Social condition associated with the guilt effect.

A.claim: Connectivity between the left anterior insula seed and a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus at the time of choice varied with condition and choice, being highest when participants made Risky choices for themselves and Safe choices for both players (pFWE = 0.020, T = 4.34, d = 0.80, Z = 4.21, 115 voxels, peak at MNI [46 16 22]).
A.note: insula-IFG coupling varies with condition

B.claim: Connectivity between the left anterior insula seed and a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus at the time of choice varied with condition and choice, being highest when participants made Risky choices for themselves and Safe choices for both players (pFWE = 0.020, T = 4.34, d = 0.80, Z = 4.21, 115 voxels, peak at MNI [46 16 22]).
B.note: insula-IFG coupling varies with condition

rows.claim: Anterior insula BOLD activity is significantly elevated in the Social condition compared to the Partner condition specifically after negative partner outcomes, tracking the guilt effect (responsibility-contingent partner unhappiness).

A.claim: A mass-univariate, voxel-wise analysis found a cluster within the left anterior insula ROI with higher responses to low lottery outcomes for the partner if these resulted from participant rather than partner choices (peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, peak at [–28 24 –4]).
A.note: insula higher for participant-caused low partner outcomes

B.claim: A mass-univariate, voxel-wise analysis found a cluster within the left anterior insula ROI with higher responses to low lottery outcomes for the partner if these resulted from participant rather than partner choices (peak T = 3.95, d = 0.59, 22 voxels, peak at [–28 24 –4]).
B.note: insula higher for participant-caused low partner outcomes

rows.claim: Yu and Koban (with colleagues) trained a whole-brain multivariate SVM to decode interpersonal guilt from fMRI activity patterns and derived a voxel-weight map — the "guilt signature" — that generalizes across guilt-inducing paradigms. The signature loads most strongly on anterior insula, medial prefrontal, and surrounding regions and has been validated as a pattern-level neural marker of guilt states across independent samples.

B.claim: A multivariate guilt-related brain signature (GRBS) was derived by re-analysing two previous neuroimaging studies of guilt (Yu et al., 2020).
B.note: signature derived from prior guilt studies

rows.claim: Probability of lottery selection increases with expected value advantage in both Study 1 (t(4796)=9.26, p<3.1e-20, β=0.074, 95%CI [0.059-0.090]) and Study 2 (t(3829)=10.62, p<5.3e-26, β=0.093, 95%CI [0.075-0.110]), confirming participants were sensitive to expected value in their choices.

A.claim: In Study 1, participants' probability of choosing the risky lottery increased with the difference between the expected value of the lottery and the value of the safe option (t(4796) = 9.26, p < 3.1e–20, β = 0.074).
A.note: choice increases with EV difference, same stats

B.claim: In Study 1, participants' probability of choosing the risky lottery increased with the difference between the expected value of the lottery and the value of the safe option (t(4796) = 9.26, p < 3.1e–20, β = 0.074).
B.note: choice increases with EV difference, same stats

rows.claim: The experiment partner's decisions were in fact made by an expected-value-maximizing algorithm (lottery chosen if EV_diff > 0), not by a real person, but participants were not informed of this; this deception is a structural assumption underlying all social comparison contrasts and the claim that participants felt interpersonal guilt toward a real partner.

A.claim: The partner's choices were not made by a free agent but generated by a deterministic algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value.
A.note: partner was EV-maximizing algorithm

B.claim: The partner's choices were not made by a free agent but generated by a deterministic algorithm that always selected the option with the highest expected value.
B.note: partner was EV-maximizing algorithm

rows.claim: Three clusters — precuneus (d=0.79), left temporoparietal junction (TPJ; d=0.59), and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC; d=0.54) — show greater BOLD response when participants decide for themselves and their partner (Social condition) than for themselves alone (Solo condition), replicating the association of these regions with social decision-making.

A.claim: The precuneus (d = 0.79), left temporo-parietal junction (d = 0.59), and medial prefrontal cortex (d = 0.54) were more engaged during decisions in the Social than in the Solo condition.
A.note: same three clusters, Social vs Solo

B.claim: The precuneus (d = 0.79), left temporo-parietal junction (d = 0.59), and medial prefrontal cortex (d = 0.54) were more engaged during decisions in the Social than in the Solo condition.
B.note: same three clusters, Social vs Solo

rows.claim: If interpersonal guilt is a real affective phenomenon contingent on responsibility, then in a within-subject lottery paradigm where the same partner outcomes occur under Social and Partner conditions, momentary happiness should drop more after negative partner outcomes in Social trials (participant chose) than in Partner trials (partner chose). This is operationalised as a positive interaction term between partnerWon (low partner outcome) and subjDecided (Social condition) in a mixed-effects regression of happiness on outcomes and responsibility.

A.claim: If participants feel interpersonal guilt, happiness reported after low lottery outcomes for the partner should be lower when the participant rather than the partner made the choice.
A.note: same if-then behavioural guilt prediction

B.claim: If participants feel interpersonal guilt, happiness reported after low lottery outcomes for the partner should be lower when the participant rather than the partner made the choice.
B.note: same if-then behavioural guilt prediction

rows.claim: If anterior insula encodes interpersonal guilt, then in the trial-level GLM, anterior insula BOLD should be elevated in the Social vs Partner contrast specifically after negative partner outcomes — i.e., the (condition × partner-outcome) interaction should yield a significant positive cluster in the anterior insula, detectable with small-volume FWE correction (SVC) over an a priori anterior-insula ROI derived from prior literature. The signal should not be present for the same contrast after positive partner outcomes (specificity).

B.claim: If the left anterior insula supports interpersonal guilt, then it should respond more strongly to low lottery outcomes for the partner when these follow the participant's own choice than when they follow the partner's choice.
B.note: same if-then insula guilt prediction

rows.claim: If happiness incorporates partner reward prediction errors with a responsibility-weighted rule, then a computational model of happiness that includes a social_pRPE regressor (partner RPE × subject-decided indicator) should fit participant happiness ratings better than nested alternatives that omit the responsibility interaction. Formally: the Responsibility model (and Responsibility Redux model) should achieve lower cross-validated error than baseline (own-reward-only) and additive social-utility models in both Study 1 and Study 2; and the fitted social_pRPE weight should be significantly greater than zero.

A.claim: Among five computational models fitted to momentary happiness data, the four-parameter Responsibility Redux model achieved the lowest AIC in both studies (–1499 and –1195) with mean adjusted R2 of 0.331 and 0.379, while the five-parameter Responsibility model reached the highest mean R2 (0.370 and 0.433).
A.note: responsibility models win model comparison

B.claim: If responsibility for a partner's outcomes influences momentary happiness, then a happiness model containing separate terms for the partner's reward prediction errors arising from participant versus partner choices should fit the happiness data better than models containing only own-reward and inequality terms.
B.note: responsibility model should outfit alternatives

rows.claim: If superior temporal sulcus represents the partner's affective experience selectively under responsibility, then in a model-based GLM with trial-by-trial partner RPE regressors split by who-chose, the parametric modulator for partner RPE in Social trials (subject-decided) should yield a significant cluster in left STS, while the parametric modulator for partner RPE in Partner trials (partner-decided) should not. This conditional engagement, rather than a main effect of partner RPE, is the diagnostic prediction.

B.claim: If a brain region tracks the consequences of the participant's own decisions for their partner, then it should respond more to the partner's reward prediction errors that follow participant choices than to those that follow partner choices.
B.note: region should prefer participant-caused partner RPEs

rows.claim: A computational model incorporating responsibility-modulated happiness better accounts for the behavioral guilt effect than models without responsibility weighting, providing formal parameterization of the social decision-making component.

A.claim: A likelihood ratio test showed that the Responsibility model fitted the happiness data better than all the other models, including the Responsibility Redux model (Study 1: all LR ≥ 47.36, p < 0.0001; Study 2: all LR ≥ 77.83, p < 0.0001).
A.note: responsibility model fits happiness best

B.claim: A likelihood ratio test showed that the Responsibility model fitted the happiness data better than all the other models, including the Responsibility Redux model (Study 1: all LR ≥ 47.36, p < 0.0001; Study 2: all LR ≥ 77.83, p < 0.0001).
B.note: responsibility model fits happiness best

rows.claim: Risk premiums do not differ between Solo and Social conditions in either study (Study 1: t(39)=1.53, p=0.134, Cohen's d=0.24, BF10=0.49; Study 2: t(43)=−0.21, p=0.84, d=−0.03, BF10=0.17), providing evidence against social-context-driven changes in risk aversion in this paradigm.

A.claim: In Study 1, risk premiums did not differ between the Solo and Social conditions (t(39) = 1.53, p = 0.134, Cohen's d = 0.24, BF10 = 0.49).
A.note: null risk premium Solo vs Social

B.claim: In Study 1, risk premiums did not differ between the Solo and Social conditions (t(39) = 1.53, p = 0.134, Cohen's d = 0.24, BF10 = 0.49).
B.note: null risk premium Solo vs Social

rows.claim: All findings are scoped to a two-study design: Study 1 is an fMRI study of N=40 young adults run on a 3T scanner using a within-subject lottery paradigm with three conditions (Solo, Social, Partner) over two scanning sessions; Study 2 is a behavioural-only replication with N=44 independent participants using the same task outside the scanner. Both studies use the same EV-maximising algorithmic partner (the participants are not told the partner is an algorithm). All neural claims derive from Study 1; all behavioural claims are tested in both studies. Conclusions about interpersonal guilt are conditional on this paradigm — repeated lottery decisions in a constrained risk-taking design with monetary stakes — and on the specific population sampled.

A.claim: All findings rest on two separate samples — a behaviour-only study of 40 participants and an fMRI study of 44 participants — analysed separately rather than pooled.
A.note: two separate samples analysed separately

B.claim: All findings rest on two separate samples — a behaviour-only study of 40 participants and an fMRI study of 44 participants — analysed separately rather than pooled.
B.note: two separate samples analysed separately

rows.claim: The weight on partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant choices (social_pRPE) is significantly greater than zero in both the Responsibility model (Study 1: Z=2.85, p=0.004; Study 2: Z=3.26, p=0.001) and the Responsibility Redux model (Study 1: Z=2.93, p=0.003; Study 2: Z=3.30, p=0.001), demonstrating that participant-caused partner RPEs independently influence participant happiness.

A.claim: The partner's reward prediction errors resulting from the participant's own decisions — those for which participants were responsible — contributed to explaining changes in participants' momentary happiness (weights for social_pRPE greater than 0: Study 1: Z = 2.85, p = 0.004; Study 2: Z = 3.26, p = 0.001).
A.note: social_pRPE weight above zero, same Z

B.claim: The partner's reward prediction errors resulting from the participant's own decisions — those for which participants were responsible — contributed to explaining changes in participants' momentary happiness (weights for social_pRPE greater than 0: Study 1: Z = 2.85, p = 0.004; Study 2: Z = 3.26, p = 0.001).
B.note: social_pRPE weight above zero, same Z

rows.claim: Superior temporal sulcus (STS) BOLD activity tracks partner reward prediction errors specifically when the participant was responsible for the choice, consistent with mentalizing about the partner's experiential state.

A.claim: Within brain regions sensitive to outcomes of risky choices, one cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus responded more to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices (pFWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, Z = 4.57, 100 voxels, peak at MNI [−52 –32 0]).

rows.claim: Bilateral ventral striatum activation increases with the computational model's expected certain rewards and expected values of chosen lotteries (left: pFWE=0.002, T=5.63, d=0.75, Z=5.41, 110 voxels, MNI [−14 8 −8]; right: pFWE=0.005, T=5.46, d=0.70, Z=5.26, 80 voxels, MNI [10 10 −4]), validating the model-based fMRI approach as a manipulation check before the STS analysis.

A.claim: Activation in bilateral ventral striatum increased with the amount of expected certain rewards and the expected values of chosen lotteries, as captured by a computational model-based regressor coding participant rewards (left: pFWE = 0.002, T = 5.63, d = 0.75).

B.note: striatum scales with model reward regressor

rows.claim: Bilateral ventral striatum shows greater BOLD response when participants choose the risky (lottery) rather than safe option, irrespective of Social or Solo condition (left cluster: Cohen's d=0.72; right cluster: d=0.85), replicating established striatal responses to risky decision-making.

A.claim: Bilateral ventral striatum was engaged more when participants chose the risky rather than the safe option, irrespective of Social or Solo condition (Cohen's d = 0.72 and 0.85 in the left and right clusters), replicating previous findings.
A.note: striatum greater for risky than safe

B.claim: Bilateral ventral striatum was engaged more when participants chose the risky rather than the safe option, irrespective of Social or Solo condition (Cohen's d = 0.72 and 0.85 in the left and right clusters), replicating previous findings.

extras.claim: Medians of the forgetting factor gamma varied little across models (0.39–0.44 in Study 1, 0.42–0.46 in Study 2), indicating stable influences of previous trials on happiness.

Parameters of the Responsibility Redux temporal difference model could be reliably recovered from synthetic happiness data generated from each participant's estimated parameters with 1SD of added noise.
The risk attitude parameter rho did not vary between gain and loss trials in either study, justifying pooling across gain and loss trials.
Risk premium and rho were highly consistent with each other across participants in both conditions and both studies.

A scripted icebreaker session was run before the task to establish a positive, non-competitive relationship, and post-task partner ratings (all above 8 on a 1–10 scale in both studies) serve as the manipulation check on that social context.

In Study 2, participants' probability of choosing the risky lottery increased with the difference between the expected value of the lottery and the value of the safe option (t(3829) = 10.62, p < 5.3e–26, β = 0.093).

Among five computational models fitted to momentary happiness data, the four-parameter Responsibility Redux model achieved the lowest AIC in both studies (–1499 and –1195) with mean adjusted R2 of 0.331 and 0.379, while the five-parameter Responsibility model reached the highest mean R2 (0.370 and 0.433).

Insula ROIs responded more to low lottery outcomes for the partner when these resulted from the participant's rather than the partner's choices, even when responses to high outcomes were subtracted, mirroring the behavioural guilt effect.

The left superior temporal sulcus cluster responded to the computational-model-based regressors coding participant reward prediction resulting from participant and partner choices in both sessions of the experiment.

Participants' own reward prediction errors influenced happiness more than the partner's reward prediction errors, whether the latter resulted from participant or partner choices (Study 1: all Z > 6.0, p < 0.001; Study 2: all Z > 3.7, p < 0.003).

Feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility evoked by social decisions under risk have identifiable neural mechanisms.
The behavioural difference in happiness following low partner outcomes after participant rather than partner choices is compatible with 'simple guilt', and is referred to as the 'guilt effect'.
The lower happiness under participant agency may reflect the drive behind responsibility aversion, perhaps the 'weight of the responsibility' of being the decider in a social setting.
This part of prefrontal cortex is sensitive to guilt-related information during social choices.
Being assigned the role of decision-maker for others in a social setting produces responsibility aversion (Edelson et al., 2018).

Changes in momentary happiness during a probabilistic reward task are explained by the combined influence of recent reward expectations and the prediction errors arising from those expectations (Rutledge et al., 2014; Rutledge et al., 2016).

With the exception of the superior temporal sulcus, the regions responding more to lottery than to safe-choice outcomes — anterior insula, dorsal mPFC, ventral striatum, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and inferior parietal lobe — have previously been associated with the processing of risk and/or ambiguity (Wu et al., 2021).
Inequality between rewards received by oneself and by another influences well-being (Loewenstein et al., 1989).

Prior functional connectivity work reports differences in the networks engaged by social versus self-only choices (Jung et al., 2013; Ogawa et al., 2018), midbrain–anterior cingulate interactions during compensation for guilt (Yu et al., 2014), and a link between insula connectivity and responsibility aversion (Edelson et al., 2018).
These results replicate the finding that outcomes of risky social decisions influence momentary happiness (Rutledge et al., 2016).
Risk attitudes differ between gains and losses (Kahneman and Tversky, 1979).
'Simple guilt' is the aversive state arising when an agent believes they have let down another party's expectations through their own choice (Battigalli and Dufwenberg, 2007).

The BOLD analysis of computational variables uses regressors whose amplitudes come from the happiness model already fitted to the same participants' ratings.
The connectivity analyses seed from clusters defined by group-level contrasts in the same dataset, with a single fixed seed applied to every participant.

Five happiness models are compared, and the family is constructed so that responsibility-based accounts are tested against inequality-based accounts inherited from prior work, with the fifth model derived after inspecting these data.
The fMRI sample size was fixed in advance by a power analysis anchored to the Study 1 effect size, not by data-dependent stopping.
The lottery was resolved independently for participant and partner, so outcome inequality and partner prediction error are dissociable by design rather than by post hoc modelling.
Model selection among the happiness models rests on within-sample fit indices and pairwise likelihood ratio tests, with no cross-validation or held-out data.

Momentary happiness was sampled only on every second trial and Z-scored within participant, so the happiness models fit relative within-subject fluctuation at half the trial resolution, not absolute well-being.

Participants chose between a safe monetary option and a risky lottery with equally probable high and low outcomes under three conditions (Solo, Social, Partner), where choices in the Social and Partner conditions led to outcomes affecting both players.

Risk attitude is estimated by two routes — a model-free risk premium from a logistic fit and a CARA exponential-utility parameter fitted by probit regression — applied separately to Solo and Social conditions.
The ROI mixed-model analyses of BOLD treat individual voxels as observations with subject as the only random factor, giving observation counts in the tens to hundreds of thousands.
Whole-brain imaging inference is thresholded at cluster-level FWE p < 0.05 with a cluster-forming threshold of p < 0.001 uncorrected, with small-volume correction used only where explicitly stated.

If choosing for a partner as well as oneself changes risk preferences, then the risk premium — the difference between a lottery's expected value and its certainty equivalent — should differ between the Social and the Solo condition.
If choosing for a partner as well as oneself changes risk preferences, then the expected-utility risk-aversion parameter rho should differ between the Social and the Solo condition.
If choosing for a partner as well as oneself changes risk preferences, then the proportion of risky (lottery) choices should differ between the Social and the Solo condition.

If deciding on behalf of a partner recruits social-cognitive processing, then regions previously associated with social cognition should be more engaged during Social than Solo decisions, and most engaged when the participant chooses the risky option in the Social condition.

If the happiness decrease reflects responsibility-driven guilt rather than inequality aversion or a general effect of agency, then it should appear only for low outcomes for the partner, and should appear whether or not the participant themselves received the high outcome.

If the insula and superior temporal sulcus convey guilt- and responsibility-related information to prefrontal cortex at the time of choice, then their connectivity with prefrontal regions should show a significant interaction between experimental condition and choice type.

If the neural response to low partner outcomes following participant choices reflects guilt, then it should align positively with the independently derived guilt-related brain signature, and the strength of that alignment should covary across individuals with the size of their behavioural guilt effect.

Participants' momentary happiness is influenced not only by rewards obtained in the current trial but also by expected rewards, reward prediction errors, rewards received in previous trials, and differences between rewards obtained by the participant and the partner.
Everything measured is choice behaviour, self-reported happiness, and BOLD correlation; no variable is experimentally manipulated except who made the decision and for whom.
In the fMRI study the social partner was one of two experimenters rather than a naive peer, unlike in the behavioural study where partners were paired participants.
Four of the 44 fMRI participants were excluded from the imaging analysis for excessive head motion, so behavioural and imaging analyses in Study 2 do not run on identical samples.
Scanning run is a significant factor in several ROI models, meaning some reported BOLD effects varied across the two sessions, and this instability is left undiscussed.
Stakes are small monetary amounts in the range of tens of cents, played out per trial.
These findings identify neural mechanisms of guilt and social responsibility during social decisions under risk.
The guilt effect was associated with a BOLD signal increase in the left anterior insula.
